item.title: A Nonjudgmental Space to be Judgmental
item.description:
Therapy

A Nonjudgmental Space to be Judgmental

Embracing your judgmental nature in therapy.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • Therapy is a safe space to overcome the stigma against our judgmental nature.
  • Judgments provide important information about the safety of others and situations.
  • Judgments often follow from pain or an interpersonal slight.
  • We must understand where are judgments are coming from, but also listen to rather than dismiss them.

There is a tyranny of positivity in the U.S. A belief most of us are socialized with is that it is not okay to feel sad. Therapists are tasked with counteracting the emotional phobia of the general culture when it comes to any feelings that are not happiness. One manifestation of this belief system that I see in my clinical practice is that it is not okay to have judgments.

Mizock states that therapy is a nonjudgmental space to be judgmental.
Source: Original illustration created with AI (ChatGPT/OpenAI), 2026.

Little did I know that embracing judgment would be so therapeutic for my clients. Over the years, I have encouraged my clients to confide in me their opinions, their criticisms, and their negativity. Many responded with great hesitation for fear of being seen as judgmental. Soon, I was proselytizing: “Therapy is a nonjudgmental space to be judgmental!” In fact, I believe your judgments can be very helpful.

For one, there is an evolutionary purpose to judgments. It is valuable information when we sense that someone might be hurtful and rejecting, competitive and dismissive, or narcissistic and inauthentic. This information tells us if it is safe to get closer to someone. Judgments contain precious signals about danger and risk that have aided our survival.

Fields outside of psychology have recognized the value of judgment. Self-help book titles continue to reveal our cultural suspicion of judgment, with titles like The Judgment Trap and Judgment Detox. However, business authors portray judgment as crucial to high-level leadership, with titles like Judgment: How Winning Leaders Make Great Calls. There is also a robust literature on the usefulness of judgment in law and juror decision-making.

Fear of evaluating others can lead to problems. Take a few experiences I have observed professionally. Some women are afraid to date out of fear of judging potential suitors. Others shy away from judging their spouses who, in fact, were cheating. Women, in particular, may be taught to suppress their judgments of men as an unconscious manifestation of misogyny. I have also seen men who continue to repeat harmful behavior from their childhood because they fear criticizing the way their parents implanted this behavior in them.

This is not to say that judgment does not require examination. Donald Rothberg offers a meditation seminar at the Spirit Rock center called “Transforming the Judgmental Mind.” In his training, he notes that judgment usually follows pain. He gave an example of a supervisor who dismissed a concern he raised in a meeting, which led him to feel strong judgments of him. Noting the injury that precedes a judgment can be enlightening. However, these judgments often form from reasonable experience – an unsupportive boss should be related to with caution.

As I come into my middle age with a growing self-trust, I’ve learned to take my judgments more seriously. It is still important to understand where our judgments come from – are they a projection of our own issues or a reflection of a realistic concern? Ultimately, we must allow our judgments to form, and use them to inform our right action.

item.title: Are You Threatening Me?
item.description:
First Impressions

Are You Threatening Me?

The quiet menace of the blank face.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • People often see emotions in faces where none may be present.
  • Emotion perception of neutral faces may have differing consequences for men and women.
  • Not every facial expression is meant for others—resist over-interpreting neutral faces.

I have been thinking about faces again—what they say, what we see in them, and how closely those two things are related. As someone who frequently hears things like “what are you mad about?” and “you look like you want to say something” (derogatory) when I feel as though my mind is in a nearly blank, nirvana-esque state, I have a particular personal interest in the topic. Some of my best friends have told me they were convinced I hated them before they got to know me. Years ago, our culture referred to my condition using a moderately profane (and pretty clearly misogynistic) abbreviation for my condition: RBF. I guess for me, maybe we can call it Resting Bastard Face?

In any case, the eleven of you who follow my work may know that my interest in phenomena such as these is also professional. I have published work in which I examine personality judgments made from photographs of faces (e.g., Beer, 2013, 2014), and I am far from alone in my interest in what can be conveyed by the face (e.g., Naumann et al., 2009; Engell, Todorov, & Haxby, 2010). Rather than recapitulate some of these findings (in short, there is some evidence that your level of extraversion is somewhere in your face, somehow), I think it may be instructive for our current purposes to instead summarize some anecdotes from doing this kind of work.

Reactions to "Neutral" Faces

Source: Mart Productions/Pexels

Years ago, as part of an ambitious (and thus only partially completed) project, I asked research participants to pose for 6 photographs in which they were asked to look, separately: happy, sad, angry, surprised, afraid, and neutral. The idea was that I would use these photos in future studies of personality judgment, and I did. In my first large scale study using these photos I decided to display the neutral expression to participants. This was an effort to reduce problems with individual differences in expressivity/direction-following/theatrical training/etc. I believe it was at the end of my very first session, during the debriefing—in which I explain why we’ve been here for an hour looking at photos of strangers and quietly judging them—that I first heard the question I would hear many times going forward: “Interesting. Ok, so why were they all mad?”

I frantically dug through my photo database to ensure that I had not made some terrible mistake in either selecting or labeling the photographs. I had not. I had indeed provided the “neutral” photographs. So why were they all mad? Or, why did they look mad enough that the question from the participant (and my own quick look at the photos) made me doubt my clerical and managerial abilities? I wasn’t sure, and in the years since, my stock answer has been, basically: “I don’t know, but you're not alone in seeing it this way—they believe this is their neutral face.”

Technical Terms

Knowing that psychologists love to examine pop culture phenomena, I went searching for literature on the topic. My first discovery was that the condition formerly known as RBF is now called PRNE (Perceived Resting Negative Emotion). I know, boring, but more accurate in that it specifies that this is a perception (not necessarily reality) and a gender-neutral phenomenon. Hester (2018) demonstrated some interesting effects regarding PRNE by examining ratings of neutral photos from the Chicago Face Database (CFD; Ma, Correll, & Wittenbrink, 2015). The author calculated a PRNE score from the impressions that coders had of the presence of negative (or positive) emotions in these neutral photos and connected these scores to ratings of both threat and attractiveness in men and women. They found that:

“PRNE negatively predicts attractiveness, especially for female targets, and positively predicts threat, especially for male targets. Furthermore, threat may account for why PRNE predicts attractiveness more strongly for women; female targets with greater PRNE seem more threatening and thus less attractive (for male targets, threat is unrelated to attractiveness).”

Basically, the RBF slur implies unattractiveness, but the route may be via threat. Perceived negative emotions may arouse perceived threat (hard to say which has primacy from this design and analysis) when viewing both men and women, but it is only in women that that “threatening” can morph into “unattractive”. This may explain why my friends said they thought I wanted to harm them but not that I was ugly. They at least didn’t say that other part out loud.

A Hypothesis Unsupported

Source: Ike Louie Natividad/Pexels

While I was unsurprised to see that psychologists had been tackling this question, my particular interest was actually somehow more boring than the above investigation. I was curious about the extent to which we simply perceive neutral faces as “negative,” with my lay hypothesis being something along the lines of the big reveal in The Walking Dead: that we are all infected with RBF (or RTF? Resting Threat Face?), at least to some extent. Perhaps it should just be called RF.

Luckily, the CFD provides norms for perceived emotions in neutral photos. The average neutral face scores about 2.5 for the various negative emotions rated in the CFD (e.g., anger) on a 1 (not at all) to 7 (extremely) scale (Ma et al., 2015). But this number is the same for ratings of happiness in neutral faces. So while neutral expressions do not convey zero emotion at all, my theory (shared by many of my study participants) that all resting faces are angry is likely unsupported. Perhaps my batch of 218 photographed participants were particularly high in PRNE, or perhaps the perceivers expected the people in the photos to be smiling—as people often do in photos—and the violation was jarring.

Relatedly, I would suggest that viewing a resting face in the wild is actually…rather uncommon. Both conscious observance of social norms and a lifetime of conditioning should mean that when we are engaging with others, our faces do…something…anything…most of the time. Hence, viewing a resting or neutral face might just mean the individual is currently disengaged, perhaps even at a moment when you expect them to be engaged. Somehow, this is threatening. And I guess if you are a woman, unattractive. I suppose if you are a woman who receives the dreaded “smile more, honey” greeting from a strange man, just understand that this is coming from a place of fear. Perhaps what he sees is Resting Power Face. I also suppose one protective solution for all of us would, unfortunately, be to pose a smile at all times, but I think this has the potential to backfire in numerous ways (my fake smile may be more threatening than my neutral face, to be honest). So my advice would instead be for perceivers: Sometimes faces aren’t for you. Resist the urge to interpret. Be open to the possibility of nirvana behind the eyes of strangers.
